has_capability_def.def:
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION private.has_capability(p_capability text, p_party_id uuid DEFAULT NULL::uuid)
 RETURNS boolean
 LANGUAGE sql
 STABLE SECURITY DEFINER
 SET search_path TO ''
AS $function$
  -- ARM 1 — the role grant. Byte-identical to
  -- `20260807000000_capability_model.sql:209-216`.
  select exists (
    select 1
    from public.profiles p
    join private.role_capabilities rc on rc.role = p.role
    where p.id = (select auth.uid())
      and rc.capability = p_capability
      and (not rc.requires_approved or p.status = 'approved')
  )
  -- ARM 2 — the per-night assignment. A subject holds a capability if ANY
  -- source says so, and this is the second and last source today.
  or exists (
    select 1
    from public.party_assignments pa
    -- ASSIGN-01, and it is the FIRST condition on purpose. Every existing
    -- caller passes no night, so this is what keeps one night's assignment
    -- from becoming a permission everywhere. See the paragraph above.
    where p_party_id is not null
      and pa.party_id = p_party_id
      and pa.user_id = (select auth.uid())
      and pa.capability = p_capability
      -- ASSIGN-03: a revocation is a row that was updated, never one that was
      -- removed.
      and pa.revoked_at is null
      -- ASSIGN-02, on the server's clock, which no device can move.
      and now() < pa.ends_at
  );
$function$

has_capability_def__query: select p.prosecdef, p.provolatile, p.proconfig::text, pg_get_functiondef(p.oid) as def from pg_proc p join pg_namespace n on n.oid = p.pronamespace where n.nspname = 'private' and p.proname = 'has_capability'
messages_grants_note: messages_grants came back EMPTY, and that is an artefact of the probe, not a fact about the table. information_schema.role_table_grants only shows grants where the current user is the grantor, the grantee, or a member of the grantee role; read_only: true runs as supabase_read_only_user, which is none of those for anon/authenticated. The unfiltered answer is in messages_acl / messages_acl_expanded, read from pg_class.relacl. Recorded rather than corrected in place, so a later reader does not repeat the same empty probe and read it as "no grants exist".
realtime_config_note: private_only is NOT returned by GET /v1/projects/{ref}/config/realtime — the keys above are everything the endpoint echoes back. Recording its absence is the honest form: a later claim that private_only was applied needs a behavioural proof (attempt a public join, observe PrivateOnly), never this key.

emit_path.finding: The four trigger wrappers of plan 38-02 MUST be SECURITY DEFINER, owned by the migration role. The measurement settles it: realtime.send is prosecdef = false — SECURITY INVOKER — so its INSERT into realtime.messages executes with the privileges of whichever role performed the write that fired the trigger, and realtime.messages has relrowsecurity = true with zero policies in the realtime schema. The plan's first case required prosecdef = true; it is false, so the second case holds. A SECURITY INVOKER wrapper would therefore have its emit refused by RLS-with-no-INSERT-policy for any writing role without rolbypassrls, realtime.send would swallow that refusal in its own EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN RAISE WARNING, the emit would never happen, no error would surface anywhere, and the 5-minute safety reload would keep every door screen looking correct — LIVE-01 silently degraded into LIVE-04. SECURITY DEFINER owned by the migration role closes it: public.door_scan_events.relowner is postgres (measured, not assumed), and postgres has rolbypassrls = true, so the definer's INSERT bypasses RLS.

finding_evidence.realtime.send proacl: {=X/supabase_realtime_admin,...} — EXECUTE is held by PUBLIC, so the definer can call it

emit_path.why_todays_write_paths_do_not_settle_it: Every write path this phase hangs a trigger on runs today through the service client — verified in src/app/(admin)/admin/events/[id]/guest-list/actions.ts:108 (getServiceClient) and the check-in route — and service_role carries rolbypassrls = true. So a SECURITY INVOKER wrapper would happen to work today. That is exactly why the measurement is worth writing down rather than the behaviour: 'it works today' is a property of the callers, not of the schema, and nothing in the database pins it. The first write path that reaches one of these four tables through a session client (authenticated, rolbypassrls = false) turns every emit on that path into silence. SECURITY DEFINER makes the wrapper's own privilege the answer, so the clause does not depend on who called it.
emit_path.event_media_paragraph_transfer: Partially, and the halves must not be conflated. The 20260809004500_event_media_party_id.sql:253-262 paragraph rests on two legs: (a) a RETURNS trigger function cannot be called directly — Postgres refuses with 0A000 — and EXECUTE is checked when the TRIGGER is created, not when it fires, so the default EXECUTE to PUBLIC grants nobody anything; (b) the function is SECURITY INVOKER and writes nothing. Leg (a) transfers verbatim: the four wrappers stay RETURNS trigger and stay unreachable over /rest/v1/rpc/. Leg (b) does NOT transfer — they are SECURITY DEFINER by this finding, and they cause a write. Plan 38-02 decides whether to carry a REVOKE pair on them anyway; this file does not decide it, it only refuses to let the two legs be quoted as one.
emit_path.F1: Regardless of the finding above, plan 38-02 also REVOKEs EXECUTE on the fan-out helper. The helper takes two uuid arguments, so it is NOT a trigger function: leg (a) does not protect it, and with the default EXECUTE to PUBLIC it is reachable over /rest/v1/rpc/ by any signed-in session, which could forge 'the list changed' on any night whose id it knows — a reload storm at a door from an ordinary account. That is finding F1, and it is closed in plan 38-02 (created in the private schema plus REVOKE ALL ... FROM public, anon, authenticated, with no re-grant), not here.
